en: // The Chapter on Mindfulness //
// Second Daily Lesson //
Nyāyabindu-pañjikā, Chapter 51: Thus, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been analyzed.
The Cārvākas, however, assert that perception (*pratyakṣa*) alone is the means of valid cognition.
Among them, some maintain that inference (*anumāna*) is included within perception.
Some, however, maintain that [the Veda] lacks authority;
namely, the followers of Kaṇāda and the Sautrāntikas, who accept only perception and inference.
Among them, the former hold that verbal testimony is included within inference.
Others, however, [assert] their inclusion [within other categories]; some [assert] their lack of authority; and those Sāṃkhyas [assert] both their [inclusion] and their scriptural authority.
And there are those who follow the Bhūṣaṇa school of thought.
Among them, the former maintained that the Veda is beginningless,
while the latter held that it was created by God.

And those [means of knowledge], along with memory, belong to the Vaiśeṣika partialists and to our own partial adherents; those same ones, together with presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), belong to the Prābhākaras;
and those same ones, with non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) as the sixth, belong to the Tautātitas.

Those who delight in the allure of that [worldly existence] are proponents of illusion (māyāvādins); those who take refuge in the Purāṇas are joined with those very things that are possible. This is the method for apprehending the acceptance of contemporary means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
In infinite past and future time, who could accept what,
or who could reject what?
Who knows this, other than that one God who directly perceives the entire cosmic cycle (*kalpa*)?
And here, those who argue for a deficiency [in the categories] have already been refuted on that occasion;
however, it must now be explained how those things accepted by others as additional are actually included [within these categories].

In this regard, just as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and the like are held to be subsumed under perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other [means of valid cognition], [so too must the additional categories be accounted for].
The same applies to others as well.
Some maintain that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) consists solely of the nature of perception (*grahaṇa*);

for instance, having raised the objection: "If even in recognition there is a distinction of parts, such that one part is memory (*smṛti*) and another is experience (*anubhava*)," Śrī Viṣṇucitta replied: "If there were a difference in the object (*viṣaya*..."
In that case, a division into parts would be possible;
for it is only oneness, which is partless, that is the object of the perception of recognition.
If it is asked how a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) can produce a direct cognition, we say: no.

Because the cognizer is one and the same, it is logical that the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), conjoined with the sense organs such as the eye, serves as the cause for the immediate cognition "this is that very thing.
That recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which takes the form "this person is indeed that same one," establishes the identity of the immediately perceived object.
Because it is produced solely from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), that [recognition] is not memory; rather, it is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Thus, it is stated in the *Dīpa* commentary on the sūtra "And because of recognition" (*anusmṛteśca*): "Furthermore, cloth and other such things are not momentary because of recognition;
for they are recognized as 'this is that very same thing.'"
Recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is indeed a single perceptual cognition whose object is a single entity existing across past and present times.
Its object is precisely that one entity as qualified by its connection with two points in time.
Furthermore, the "that" (*tad*) component is not memory.
It must be stated that this "this-portion" is indeed a perception, because there is no sensory contact with a past object;
for there is a manifestation of oneness through the perception [of the object] in grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) as "that is this."
"For a person whose sense-organ contact is accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by previous experience, such a perception is indeed possible;
for everywhere, the postulation of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) depends upon positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Others, however, considering here the refutation of the contradiction regarding the difference between cognitions, [hold that] because the conformity to the presence and absence of latent impressions is observed in the aspect of "that" (*tad-aṃśa*), it has the nature of being non-perceptual (*parokṣa-rūpatā*), whereas in the aspect of "this" (*idaṃ-aṃśa*), it has the nature of being perceptual (*pratyakṣa-rūpatā*).
They assert that it possesses a dual nature.
In their view, the definition of memory is "cognition whose manifestation depends upon mental impressions" (*saṃskāra*),
while perception is "immediate cognition" (*aparokṣajñāna*).

Because it possesses both characteristics, recognition must be admitted by all our proponents of established tenets to have a dual nature; for all cognitions, whether perceptual or otherwise, possess both the forms of being manifest and being unmanifest,
due to their self-luminosity.
Furthermore, all cognitions are direct perceptions (*pratyakṣa*) with respect to both their own objective aspect and the other [subjective] aspect.

This has also been stated by Śrī Viṣṇucitta: "Cognition is one and the same, being both self-illuminating and the illuminator of the object; in that case, how can there be a distinction between memory and experience?"

Having raised this objection, we reply: "Because there is a distinction within that which is manifesting. Just as, in a single cognition such as "this is a cow," there is a differentiation of parts of the cognition due to the distinction between the qualifier, the qualified, and the object.

For example: in the single cognition "this is a cow," there is a distinction between parts of the cognition due to the difference between the qualifier (*prakāra*) and the qualified object (*viṣaya*);
and just as in the single cognition "a pot and a cloth" there is a distinction between parts;
or as in erroneous cognitions admitted by others, there is validity regarding the part that is the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
And because of the rebuttal: "And there is a lack of authority in the other case";

likewise, having raised the objection: "Even the self-luminous portion of memory is born solely from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), since there is an absence of any other specific causes such as the sense organs," [the author replies]: "It is not so."
And because of the resolution that "the luminosity of cognitions is inherent," therefore,
in all cases, the distinction between immediacy, inferentiality, memory, and so forth, exists solely in relation to the object.
As for the confusion or non-confusion of universals (jāti), however, this is to be determined by observation and non-observation.
And it is like the confusion [of categories] arising from adventitious conditions (*aupādhika-saṃkara*).
Thus, since its dual nature is established, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is likewise of a dual nature.

Recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), like direct perception (*abhijñā*), is threefold according to the distinction of the sense organs and so forth; because it is rooted in the convergence of their respective latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), it becomes ninefold.
Let it be granted that the statement regarding direct perception (pratyakṣatā) concerns cases such as a lamp, which are intended for illustration;
for indeed, a cognition in the form "this is that" does not fail to arise through means such as inferential marks (liṅga).
Recognition arising from verbal testimony serves as the basis for its application;
and the principle established in the section concerning different recensions applies equally to ritual acts and knowledge.
Because subverting factors and the like are impossible in all cases— just as in the case of [the recognition of] lamps and so forth—
the recognized cognition under dispute is a valid means of knowledge, just like determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*).

Since there is no contradiction between the acts of performing and not performing [an action] due to limiting conditions such as differences in time, it is not possible to conceive of a distinction [between the two] in the case of a seed and so forth.
Otherwise, due to differences in location, performance, non-performance, and so forth, there would be no single entity at all in the world; thus, everything would be void.
Therefore, by means of recognition whose object is touched by contradictory [states],
the stability of selves is established, as is that of external objects in reality.
Nyāyapañcādhyāyī, Śabdanirūpaṇa 53: Synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) also has the self as its object, for it is a specific kind of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*),
having such forms as "I who saw that very same thing am now touching it."
Some maintain that "recognition" (*pratisandhi*) is a single cognition whose object consists of two things;
in that case too, it must be completed as "a single cognition having as its domain multiple objects experienced separately, produced by a single agent.
Furthermore, "corroboration" (*saṃvāda*) is a distinct class of cognition.
Thus say some; that is incorrect, because no other number [of categories] is possible.
As for what Varadaviṣṇumiśra stated: "Correspondence is a cognition whose object is a previously apprehended thing and which has words as its cause."
That too is intended merely to introduce specific technical designations for the internal subdivisions of verbal cognition;
for even when an object has already been apprehended, its status as being produced by the power of words does not disappear,
since otherwise it would follow that other means of knowledge whose scope is limited to what has already been apprehended would also be distinct from verbal cognition.
For indeed, such a cognition arises even for one who, immediately after hearing the words "this mountain possesses fire," reflects upon the smoke;
the same should be understood regarding the second [type of] yogic perception and so forth.
Furthermore, the quality of being independent and so on is equally present in inference whose object has been heard from scripture and the like.

It has been stated: "Validity, as well as difference or non-difference, is not dependent [on other means of knowledge], for otherwise it would follow that even the perception of grass and such things would be [dependent].
Why, then, is the fact that the Vedas and the Vedāntas have objects not already established by other means (aprāptaviṣayatva) being argued?
If you say this, consider the following: if it does not attain that [status], there is the consequence of its being directly invalid;

even if it does attain that status, because it would be disregarded by discerning people who fear fruitless exertion, there follows the consequence of its invalidity in terms of its result. Thus observe!

Nyāyabindu-pañjikā, Chapter 3, Verse 54: If analogy (*upamāna*) is also the cognition of similarity residing in a remembered object arising from the cognition of similarity residing in a perceived object,
then it is merely memory (*smṛti*), because there exists no such thing as "similarity" distinct from the specific configuration (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*) and other attributes of those respective things.
And because that [object] has been previously perceived and is currently being remembered,
even though the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) may be new, it— like those various usages— is conditioned by the reflection upon the specific counter-correlate.
Alternatively, whatever is similar to something else is the counter-correlative of the similarity residing in that [other];
for example, one's own two hands [are mutually similar].

Thus, once pervasion is established, [the similarity residing in the remembered object] is proven through the inference: "The cow is similar to this [object], because it is the counter-correlate of the similarity residing in this [object]. Therefore, the similarity residing in the remembered object is not unestablished.

Otherwise, the cognition of dissimilarity residing in the remembered object, arising from the knowledge of dissimilarity residing in the perceived object, would also have to be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If that [cognition of dissimilarity] is considered presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), why should the cognition of similarity not be so as well? Thus it is argued.

Alternatively, since the similarity residing in both [objects] flashes forth by the very cognition "this is similar to that" occurring simultaneously, it cannot be caused by that [previous perception].

Otherwise, what would be the explanation for two objects previously experienced separately—whose similarity was not perceived at that time—when they are later remembered simultaneously, their similarity being perceived all at once?
Or must another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) be postulated even in that case?
As is a cow, so is a gavaya;
like a cow, a horse does not have cloven hooves;
a camel is an animal with a long neck, hanging lips, and a deformed shape.
This [definition], however, concerns only those cases where the subject matter consists of similarity (*sādharmya*), dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), or the mere property (*dharma*).
All three types of analogical transfer statements (*atideśavākya*) are indeed scripture (*āgama*).

As for the claim: "Comparison (*upamāna*) is the recognition of the meaning of the transfer statement regarding a gavaya and so forth, by one who has heard the transfer statement," [this is incorrect].
And as for the claim that "this [instruction] has the result of producing proficiency," that too is untenable, because proficiency is already established beforehand.

As for the statement: “Because similarity is the basis [of the convention], and because that basis is not perceived, the convention cannot be grasped beforehand, whether by means of the word itself or even through inference.”
Thus, [the claim] that "the sign (nimitta) is not cognized therein" is unestablished;
for the specific universal (jāti), namely *gavayatva* and the like, as characterized by the form of similarity to a cow, is indeed cognized first and foremost as the meaning of the sentence.

There is first of all a cognition of that which is characterized by the form of similarity to a cow as the meaning of the sentence; for the cognition is indeed: "A certain particular individual characterized by similarity to a cow is a *gavaya*.
Subsequently, for one who has perceived the *gavaya* through direct perception, there is merely the clarification of that [cognition].
And it has been stated by the venerable Viṣṇucitta: "In the statement 'the gavaya is like a cow,' that which is denoted is a universal residing in the same locus as the similarity to a cow;

this is established because it is first understood as the meaning of the sentence. If there is no determination of that which is characterized by similarity to a cow, then there will be no determination even subsequently."
Otherwise, if there were no determination [of meaning] at that time, there would likewise be none later;
therefore, it must have been determined at the very moment the sentence was heard.
Furthermore, if this were not accepted, how could there be the acquisition of the linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) for words such as "Indra"?
For in this case, there is no perception of specific configurations and so forth that serve as causes;
nor is there a permanent lack of proficiency therein, because that would entail the impossibility of understanding the meaning of sentences qualified by those [meanings].

In this way, there would likewise be an eternal lack of linguistic convention for words such as "eternal," "supersensible object," and "mental impression" (*saṃskāra*). If, however, some means of justification can be found in those cases, the same applies here as well.
Thus it is established that comparison (*upamāna*) is not a distinct means of knowledge.
Presumption (*arthāpatti*), however, is simply inference (*anumāna*);

for instance, the postulation of a corroborating factor (*upapādaka*) based on the observation of something that would otherwise be inexplicable is nothing other than the cognition of a pervader (*vyāpaka*) from a pervaded (*vyāpya*).
Because that which is not pervaded cannot be logically established without it,
and because that which is not the pervader cannot serve as its logical establisher;
thus, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is the determination of the object when there is a conflict between two means of valid cognition.
Nor should it be said that [this is so],
because there is no contradiction between two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), nor is it possible for two contradictory things to possess the status of valid cognition.

Now, when Devadatta’s being alive has been ascertained through some means of valid cognition, there arises— without qualification— the understanding of his connection with a general location in the form, "One who is alive must exist somewhere"; and since this understanding encompasses the house as well, there is a manifest contradiction when one perceives his absence in that very house.
"Therefore, the postulation of its existence outside [the house] for the sake of its negation therein is presumptive testimony (arthāpatti)";
this is not so,
because there is no rule that living necessarily occurs only in some specific place.

Because, when there is doubt regarding external existence, the perception of absence from the house— which takes the form of a certainty— is incapable of contending with it; furthermore, there can never be a case of actual equality in strength between two cognitions of contradictory objects,
though such might somehow occur if both were equally invalid.
The same applies even when there is an equality of strength based on mere presumption;
for when a discrepancy is perceived,
since the determination of strength and weakness follows from that very perception, what remains to be established through presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*)?

Therefore, when there is the proximity of a specific [rule] that is exclusive and possesses no other scope, the general [rule] which does possess such scope must be restricted; this would be the established conclusion.
And since that [restriction] occurs in exactly the same manner as pervasion (*vyāpti*), it is indeed the very fruit of inference.

Otherwise, why should there not be the postulation of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) even in cases such as the restriction to non-contradictory particulars, just as there is in the abandonment of a contradictory object?
Furthermore, if this were not accepted, it would follow that even inferences such as that from smoke [to fire] would be cases of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*),

since one could assert both the impossibility [of the effect] without the cause (fire) and the contradiction between two means of knowledge in the form of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and perception.

For smoke implies the fire that is its cause, yet it contradicts direct perception; thus, in this contradiction, the postulation of the restriction "there is fire on the near side of the mountain" would constitute presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Without the determination of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the capacity to prove (*gamakatā*) is understood only through the connection of the prover (*gamaka*) with another property; thus, distinctions such as these are merely imagined out of wishful thinking.
And so it was said by the venerable Viṣṇutittas: "Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is inference," and so forth.
However, some apply the designation "presumption" to the purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*).
Since that [position] has already been refuted, it does not enter into the category of the means of valid cognition;
or, even if it were to enter, it would possess no distinctness [from them].

As for the inclusion of analogy (*upamāna*) and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) in passages such as "perception is preceded by the senses, logical marks, words, similarity, and things otherwise inexplicable" (*Nyāyapariśiṣṭa*, *Śabdapariccheda* 55),

that too does not constitute the final established doctrine (*siddhānta*), because it occurs within the section of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). Furthermore, in our system, non-existence (*abhāva*) is essentially a particular state of existence (*bhāvāntarātmā*).
And that [non-existence] is established by the sense organs, such as the eyes, according to their respective capacities.

Even when it is apprehended as having the nature of absence (*abhāva*), those very same [senses], accompanied by auxiliary factors such as the recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), constitute the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, there is no room for postulating anything additional to them.
For this very reason, the cognition of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), and so forth, is also fully accounted for.

For indeed, a particularity such as the connection with place, time, and so forth, having been perceived, subsequently ascends to the intellect of a person who possesses the recollection of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) in the form of its absence— or due to the non-recollection of that which ought to be recollected;
in that case, there is an inference of its absence.
Thus, even on the view that negation is a distinct entity (*atiriktābhāvapakṣa*), the postulation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) is baseless;
for just as there is the perception "the ground with a jar," there is likewise the immediate (*aparokṣā*) perception "the ground without a jar.
Nor is the sense organ exhausted merely by the apprehension of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
Because this would lead to the same consequence regarding qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth;

furthermore, since the reasons such as "being a means for what is unknown" (*ajñātakaraṇatva*) are easily available even if [the object] is not distinct [from its parts], these are indeed inferences (*anumāna*).
Possibility (*saṃbhava*) is likewise nothing but inference.
This is because statements such as "a hundred is contained within a thousand" communicate a pervasion (vyāpti) pertaining to thousands previously experienced;
whereas statements such as "valor is possible in a Kṣatriya" lack authority because they consist of doubt.

Even if [the former] were of the nature of a certainty regarding non-contradiction, that certainty would ultimately depend upon another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes that non-contradiction.

Tradition (*aitihya*), however, is an *āgama* if it is rooted in a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); if it is rooted in what appears to be such (*tadābhāsa*), then it is a semblance thereof (*tadābhāsa*).
Likewise, gestures, written characters, and so forth, being invariably concomitant with specific intended meanings or phonemes, are nothing but inference (*anumāna*).

Regarding gesture (*ceṣṭā*), the venerable Varadanārāyaṇabhaṭṭāraka has stated as follows: "For even by means of gesture, an imitation of verbal usage is indeed performed, which brings about the cognition of its own meaning for those yogins who possess verbal knowledge."
If it is your view that in beginningless linguistic conventions, gestures whose powers are already known can produce cognition just as perception does;
For either gestures or words must be accepted for the purpose of communicating with others;
in that case, since words are beginningless, their beginninglessness is superior.
Gesture is conventional, following linguistic usage;
it is established in the scriptures of Bharata and others that such gesture serves to convey understanding of this very [meaning].
“The tradition is seen to be beginningless, its author being no longer remembered,” and so forth.
However, in the *Tattvaratnākara*, it is stated thus: “If verbal activity is characterized by a fixed rule between the signifier and the signified for one who possesses linguistic proficiency...”
Even that which is indeterminate (aniyata) acts as a reminder upon being seen; therefore, it should not be considered a separate [means of knowledge].
However, regarding written characters, the cognition that "this is the letter *ga*" or "this is the letter *gha*"—insofar as it takes the form of the phoneme itself—is indeed invalid (*apramāṇa*).
The activity of those who grasp the relationship between written characters and [phonemes] proceeds with the intention: "By means of this sign, you should know this phoneme."
And from that, the pervasion (vyāpti) is established:
this script is preceded by the intention to represent these specific phonemes,
because it is a script written by a person who possesses the intention to represent these phonemes and is free from error and the like.
The formulation should be understood as being of this form: "like the script at the time of learning [it] through correct comprehension," and so forth.

As for that which was stated regarding intuition (*pratibhā*) in the *Tattvaratnākara*: "Now, might not some intuition that accords with reality be accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?"
But that [cognition] is capable of cognizing external objects independently of any external object.
It is true that excellence can arise depending on specific times, persons, and other factors; however, the distinctions among time and such are difficult for people like us to discern.
Even though this [intrinsic validity] exists, it is disregarded because it is not useful for conventional practice;
for the observed fruit of intuition (pratibhā) is the ascertainment of its own validity.
Because its purpose is fulfilled by other means, it is not scrutinized by the discerning;
yet among meritorious persons, this [vision] most frequently perceives the truth.
Therefore, Patañjali has declared that intuition (pratibhā) is also a means of valid cognition (pramā).
Thus, even that [statement] refers only to a specific type of yogic perception mentioned previously.

Now, one might object: "In this case, even that [classification] of three or four means of valid cognition is untenable, because it is more logical that there be only two, in the form of direct (pratyakṣa) and indirect (parokṣa)."
If it is argued thus, we say no, because it leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For instance: having removed one from among many, the others are treated as a single group; [and so on].
If there were a twofold determination [of existence and non-existence], the same consequence would follow even for things such as a jar.

Based on the distinction between inference and non-inference, and between verbal testimony and non-verbal testimony, you thus maintain that there are exactly two means of valid cognition; tell me, why does this not please you?
If it is argued that perception is grasped as distinct from the other two [inference and verbal testimony] because of its unique class-character (*vaijātya*),
then for us, the distinction of those two [inference and testimony] from each other and from perception is equally clear.
The state of being a knower is to be characterized by the common causes known as atom, sense-organ, mark, and word; or rather, it is characterized by the fourfold nature of recollection.
The duality that the Jains have declared— namely, "clear" and "unclear"—
is not distinct from the division between direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and indirect cognition (*parokṣa*).
Therefore, we do not dispute the fact that these two [means of knowledge] have been established as distinct;
however, it is difficult to maintain that there is only one means of knowledge for supersensible objects, because their difference has been proven.
Surely, even in perception there is a distinction based on the division between external and internal,
as well as by being divine or non-divine, and also by the differentiation of the eyes, ears, and so forth.
In the same way, why is the distinction between inference and scripture not accepted as a division of that single means of knowledge which is indirect?
"This has been answered somewhat; this was seen, this was heard, and this was inferred"—such is the common worldly saying that serves as witness here.

Since similarity can be found with something by virtue of some commonality, and dissimilarity can likewise be found everywhere by virtue of some difference, it is certainly acceptable to adopt such [a comparison] here as well.

Therefore, even on account of the division between what is called memory and direct experience, it is not appropriate to maintain that there are two means of valid cognition; thus, the very path previously described remains correct.
There are three kinds of experience, and likewise memory, which is rooted in them;
we do not disagree with this sixfold division.
Because the classification of memory— which is rooted in that [experience]— is already understood through the classification of experience itself,
they are stated as a single category.

Therefore, some ancient authorities distinguish the category of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) as being threefold, with the intention of including those [other cognitions] within their respective roots.
In this way, other matters as well should be considered. Thus [it is said].
Now, what is the use of this laborious inquiry into the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?

Even without reflecting upon the category of *pramāṇas*, the engagement with and withdrawal from worldly objects, along with their purposes and so forth, is established for humans— as it is for animals— by the force of perception, positive and negative concomitance, and the like, without any obstacle.

If it is argued that even regarding non-worldly matters, those whose understanding is satisfied by the various injunctions and their supporting texts such as the *Kalpasūtras*, what is the use of this futile deliberation which is like grinding what is already ground? We say: not so. For those who desire the subversion of reality in order to obstruct the scope [of valid knowledge], the path of means of valid cognition must be purified for the sake of establishing non-erroneousness.
And having connected this with the "Phana" chapter shown at the beginning of the work,
effort is exerted toward the valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) along with its auxiliary parts, for the sake of purifying the object of proof (sādhya-prameya).
Even by the lords of yogis, who have directly perceived all objects,
the ocean of the destruction of reality is crossed by relying on the boat of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, purity must be practiced according to the manner described above.

May that Blessed One, who is pure, whose head is the Veda (*śrutiśiras*), who is established in the ultimate conclusions of the Vedanta (*śuddhāntasiddhāntinī*), and who is auspicious, attain unimpaired visibility for the sake of establishing what is beneficial—she who, with compassion, maintains her devotion to her husband who is eternally full of rasa, and who releases all knots. May she be my perfect work.

Thus ends the chapter on Smṛti in the Nyāyapariśuddhi, among the works of the venerable Vedāntācārya Śrī Veṅkaṭanātha, the lion among poets and logicians, who is independent in all philosophical systems.
The Second Daily Lesson.
And the fourth chapter is completed.
